brief:
In Gaza, the price of your own money can run to forty percent. That is the fee human rights monitors report Palestinians are paying to informal cash brokers simply to convert the balance in their bank account — money they already own — into the physical banknotes needed to buy food, water, or medicine.

The Human Rights Foundation, which tracks financial repression worldwide in its Financial Freedom Report, has documented the machinery of this collapse. Gaza's banks have effectively ceased to function: branches destroyed or shuttered, ATMs dead, and inflation surging as high as 240 percent. Depositors report that the Bank of Palestine froze accounts without warning, leaving families unable to reach their savings at the moment they needed them most. Into the vacuum stepped unofficial cash brokers, who now govern access to money itself — at rates that can consume nearly half of whatever a family has left.

Set this beside the West Bank's mirror-image crisis, which this section has reported: banks there are drowning in physical shekels that Israel caps from re-entering its financial system, while Gaza's population is starving for the same banknotes. One half of Palestine cannot deposit cash; the other half cannot withdraw it. In both cases the failure is not the Palestinians' money — it is the system that stands between them and it.

This is the precise failure that the global financial-freedom movement exists to answer. When an account can be frozen without warning, self-custody — holding value that no institution can lock — stops being an ideology and becomes a household precaution. When converting your own balance costs forty percent, a remittance that arrives directly, phone to phone, at the cost of pennies is not speculation; it is arithmetic. Bitcoin's advocates have long argued it serves people failed by their banking systems. Few places on earth test that claim more brutally than Gaza in 2026.

None of this is a cure for the underlying siege, and no honest observer claims otherwise. Electricity and connectivity are scarce in Gaza; converting digital value to physical goods still requires functioning markets; and any tool can be misused. But the measure of a financial lifeline is not whether it is perfect. It is whether it is better than a frozen account, a dead ATM, and a broker taking forty percent.

The Times of Palestine Financial Freedom section will keep following both ledgers: the official system as it fails Palestinians on both sides of the Green Line, and the alternatives Palestinians are reaching for as it does.
